questions.q: What happens to an unquoted identifier like 'employees' on Oracle?
options: It's automatically folded to uppercase (EMPLOYEES)
It's automatically folded to lowercase
It stays exactly as typed with no folding
Oracle rejects unquoted identifiers entirely
questions.explain: Oracle folds unquoted identifiers to UPPERCASE automatically, so 'employees' and 'EMPLOYEES' refer to the same object.

questions.q: What happens to an unquoted identifier like 'Employees' on PostgreSQL?
options: It's automatically folded to lowercase (employees)
It's automatically folded to uppercase
It stays exactly as typed
PostgreSQL rejects unquoted identifiers entirely
questions.explain: PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lowercase automatically, the opposite direction from Oracle.

questions.q: Why might the genuinely messy case-sensitivity of MySQL table names vary between two MySQL servers running the exact same CREATE TABLE statement?
options: Because MySQL maps tables to files on disk, so table-name case sensitivity can depend on whether the underlying OS filesystem (e.g. Linux vs. Windows) is case-sensitive
Because MySQL randomly assigns case sensitivity at install time
Because MySQL always behaves identically regardless of OS
Because case sensitivity in MySQL depends only on the SQL client, never the server
questions.explain: MySQL's default storage behavior maps tables to filesystem files, so table/database name case-sensitivity can depend on the OS filesystem of the server running it.

questions.q: Why would 'SELECT * FROM "Employees"' fail on PostgreSQL if the table was originally created unquoted as 'CREATE TABLE Employees (...)' ?
options: Because the unquoted creation folded the name to lowercase 'employees', but the quoted query literally looks for 'Employees' with a capital E
Because PostgreSQL never allows double-quoted table references
Because PostgreSQL requires all table names to be in uppercase
Because CREATE TABLE and SELECT must always use identical quoting styles or PostgreSQL throws a syntax error
questions.explain: The unquoted CREATE TABLE folded the name to lowercase 'employees'. The quoted SELECT looks for the literal, case-sensitive 'Employees', which doesn't exist — a classic source of 'table not found' confusion.

questions.q: On SQL Server, what actually determines whether unquoted identifier comparisons are case-insensitive?
options: The database/column collation setting (most default collations are case-insensitive)
It's a hard-coded language rule with no exceptions
The version of SQL Server Management Studio being used
Whether the query uses brackets or not
questions.explain: Case sensitivity on SQL Server is controlled by collation. Most default collations are case-insensitive (CI), but a database could be created with a case-sensitive collation instead.
